questions.question: What is a vector database?

options.text: A database optimized for storing and searching high-dimensional vectors (embeddings)

questions.explanation: Vector databases store and index high-dimensional vectors (embeddings from ML models). Enable similarity search: find vectors closest to a query vector. Examples: Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, pgvector.

questions.question: What is a vector embedding?

options.text: A numerical representation of data (text, images, etc.) in high-dimensional space where similar items are close together

questions.explanation: Embeddings: ML models convert data to vectors. 'cat' and 'kitten' have similar vectors, far from 'car'. Dimensions: 100s to 1000s. Captures semantic meaning. Foundation for similarity search.

questions.question: What is similarity search in vector databases?

options.text: Finding vectors closest to a query vector using distance metrics like cosine similarity or Euclidean distance

questions.explanation: Similarity search: given query vector, find k nearest neighbors. Distance metrics: cosine similarity (angle), Euclidean (straight-line), dot product. Returns semantically similar items, not exact matches.

questions.question: What are common use cases for vector databases?
questions.explanation: Vector DB use cases: semantic search (find similar documents), recommendations (similar products/content), RAG (retrieve context for LLMs), image search, anomaly detection, deduplication.

questions.question: What is ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) search?

options.text: Trading perfect accuracy for speed—finding approximately nearest vectors much faster than exact search

questions.explanation: Exact nearest neighbor: O(n) scan all vectors. ANN: use indexes (HNSW, IVF) to find approximate results in O(log n). 95%+ recall with 100x+ speedup. Essential for large-scale vector search.

questions.question: What is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)?

options.text: A graph-based index structure for efficient approximate nearest neighbor search

questions.explanation: HNSW: builds a multi-layer graph. Higher layers: long-range connections for fast navigation. Lower layers: dense connections for accuracy. State-of-the-art ANN index. Used by most vector DBs.

questions.question: What is RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)?

options.text: Using vector search to retrieve relevant context, then feeding it to an LLM for generation

questions.explanation: RAG: embed documents in vector DB, embed user query, retrieve similar documents, include in LLM prompt. Grounds LLM responses in your data. Reduces hallucinations. Key pattern for enterprise AI.

questions.question: What is the difference between cosine similarity and Euclidean distance?

options.text: Cosine: measures angle (direction); Euclidean: measures straight-line distance (magnitude matters)

questions.explanation: Cosine similarity: angle between vectors, ignores magnitude. Good for text (document length shouldn't matter). Euclidean: actual distance, magnitude matters. Choose based on whether magnitude is meaningful.

questions.question: Which of these is a vector database?
questions.explanation: Pinecone: managed vector DB. Milvus: open-source, scalable. Weaviate: open-source with built-in vectorization. Also: Qdrant, Chroma, pgvector (PostgreSQL extension). Growing ecosystem.

questions.question: What is metadata filtering in vector databases?

options.text: Combining vector similarity search with traditional filters (e.g., category='electronics' AND similar to query)

questions.explanation: Metadata filtering: hybrid queries. 'Find similar products WHERE category='electronics' AND price < 100'. Combines semantic similarity with structured filters. Essential for real applications.

questions.question: What challenge do vector databases face with high-dimensional data?

options.text: Curse of dimensionality—distances become less meaningful, indexes less effective in very high dimensions

questions.explanation: Curse of dimensionality: in very high dimensions, all points become roughly equidistant. ANN indexes lose effectiveness. Solutions: dimensionality reduction, better embedding models, specialized indexes.

questions.question: A company wants to build a 'find similar products' feature using product images. What's the approach?

options.text: Store images in a relational database
Generate image embeddings with a vision model, store in vector DB, query with embedding of input image

questions.explanation: Image similarity: use vision model (CLIP, ResNet) to generate embeddings. Store in vector DB. Query: embed input image, find nearest neighbors. Returns visually similar products. No manual tagging needed.
